segments.voice: Yesterday, the saints: not statues, people who fell and kept going. Your line was: the company you're in. Today we meet one of them up close. Day eight.

segments.voice: Italy, the Middle Ages. A town on a hill called Assisi. There's a young man there everyone knows: the son of a rich cloth merchant, good clothes, good parties, the one who pays for everybody's dinner. He dreams of being a knight. He goes off to a war with the next town, gets captured, spends a long stretch in a prison cell, and comes home sick. And something in him has changed. He starts giving things away. Money, cloth from his father's shop. His father is furious, and drags him in front of the bishop of Assisi, in the town square, to get his property back. What the son does next is why people still know his name.
screen: `ASSISI, A TOWN ON A HILL.` → `THE RICH MERCHANT'S SON.` → `DRAGGED BEFORE THE BISHOP.`

segments.voice: His name was Francesco. We say Francis. According to the stories written down by his early followers, he stood in front of the bishop and the whole town, took off his clothes, every piece, and handed them back to his father. And he said, in effect: until now I called you my father. From now on I'll say our Father, who art in heaven. The bishop covered him with his own cloak. Francis walked out of town with nothing. What came next is the part people forget. He didn't become a hermit. He went toward the people everyone avoided. The stories say that once, riding outside town, he met a man with leprosy, a disease that made people outcasts, and instead of riding past, he got down and kissed his hand. Later he wrote that what had seemed bitter to him was turned into sweetness. He rebuilt ruined chapels with his own hands. He gathered friends who lived poor, preached in the streets, and cared for the sick. They became the Franciscans, and Franciscans still carry his name today. He loved creation, too. Near the end of his life he wrote a song, the Canticle of the Creatures, praising God for brother sun and sister moon, even sister death. Now today's line: lord, make me an instrument. It opens the prayer that bears his name, make me an instrument of your peace. Here's the honest part. As far as anyone can tell, Francis didn't write it. Its first known printing is in a small French magazine, La Clochette, in 1912, with no author's name. His name was attached to it later. Francis's own words are in the Canticle. The Peace Prayer borrowed his name.

segments.voice: Here's the practice. A forty-five-second sit. Get comfortable and let your breath slow down. Think of one thing you own that you're holding on to a little too tightly. It doesn't have to be big. A grudge counts. With each breath out, imagine loosening your grip on it, the way Francis handed his clothes back. If you pray, you can say the line: lord, make me an instrument. The bell holds the time.
Francis. Francis of Assisi, the rich kid who gave it all back and went toward the outcasts. Eighth word.

9.title: why there's fire in every church
9.hook: why there's fire in every church
9.tomorrow: what the string is for (counting, not magic)
9.howItsDone: Catholics light votive candles in churches for people they are praying for, keep a sanctuary lamp burning near the tabernacle, and light the paschal candle at the Easter Vigil, baptisms and funerals.

screen: `DAY NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Francis, the rich kid who handed his clothes back. Your line was: lord, make me an instrument. What small good thing did you carry? Day nine.

segments.voice: Every building has lights now. Switches, LEDs, the glow of exit signs. And yet step into a Catholic church at noon, in a city with perfect electricity, and there's still fire. Two candles on the altar. A tall one near the front. Rows of little flames in red glass in a side corner, flickering, somebody's coins in the box beside them. And one small red lamp that never seems to go out. It isn't for seeing. Nobody needs a candle to read anymore. So why is there fire in every church? Today's word is the flame.
screen: `PERFECT ELECTRICITY.` → `AND STILL, FIRE.` → `IT ISN'T FOR SEEING.`

segments.voice: Start with what Jesus says in John's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "I am the light of the world: he that followeth me, walketh not in darkness." And in Matthew, he turns it around and says it to his listeners: "You are the light of the world." So a candle in a church is a small sermon without words. Light in the dark. And every candle you see there has its own job. The candles on or near the altar are lit for Mass. The tall one is the Easter candle, the paschal candle. On the night before Easter, Catholics gather outside in the dark, light a new fire, and carry this one candle into a black church while someone sings, three times, light of Christ. Then the flame is passed from candle to candle through the whole crowd until the room is full of light. The same candle stands near the font at baptisms, and beside the coffin at funerals. The little red lamp is the sanctuary lamp. It burns near the tabernacle, the box where the consecrated bread is kept, and Catholics keep it lit as a sign that Christ is present there. And the rows in the corner? Those are votive candles, from the Latin votum, a vow or a prayer. Someone lights one for a sick mother, a job interview, a child who's struggling, a friend who died. The flame keeps burning after they walk out the door. Some people put it this way: the candle keeps praying after I leave. In Catholic teaching, the wax does nothing by itself. It's a way of saying: this person matters, and I'm not done hoping.

segments.voice: Here's the practice. A forty-five-second sit. If there's a candle nearby, you can light it. If not, just picture one. Think of one person who could use some light right now. See their face above the flame. You don't have to fix anything. Just hold them there while it burns. If you pray, you can pray for them. The bell holds the time.
Candles. Light in the dark: the Easter candle, the sanctuary lamp, and the votive flame that keeps praying after you leave. Ninth word.

10.title: what the string is for (counting, not magic)
10.hook: what the string is for (counting, not magic)
10.tomorrow: the words, line by line, from Luke
10.howItsDone: Catholics pray the rosary alone or together, some every day, saying an Our Father, ten Hail Marys and a Glory Be for each decade while thinking about a scene from the life of Jesus and Mary.

screen: `DAY TEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, candles: the Easter flame, the red lamp, the votive that keeps burning after you leave. Your line was: light a candle for someone. Who did you think of? Day ten.

segments.voice: Maybe you've seen one hanging from a rearview mirror. Or tangled in a grandmother's purse with the car keys and the cough drops. Or in the hands of an old man on a park bench, his thumb moving one bead at a time while his lips move without a sound. A loop of beads with a small cross on the end. Some people wear them like a necklace, and some people think they're a kind of good-luck charm. They're neither, really. The string is for something much plainer and much older. It's for counting. Today, the first half of the rosary: the beads.
screen: `ON A MIRROR. IN A PURSE.` → `A THUMB, ONE BEAD AT A TIME.` → `IT'S FOR COUNTING.`

segments.voice: The word rosary comes from the Latin rosarium, a rose garden. The idea was a garland of prayers, like a crown of roses. Here's how the string is laid out. There's a cross, a few beads leading up to the loop, and then the loop itself: five groups of ten small beads, called decades, each separated by a single bead. On each single bead, people say the Our Father. On each of the ten, a Hail Mary, which is tomorrow's lesson. After each ten, a short prayer of praise called the Glory Be. So the beads keep count, and the fingers always know where they are, even in the dark, even half asleep. Why count at all? Counting prayers is ancient. Stories from the early desert monks tell of one who said three hundred prayers a day and kept track by dropping pebbles from his lap. Later, in the Middle Ages, monks prayed their way through all one hundred and fifty psalms. Tradition says ordinary people who couldn't read, or didn't own a book, prayed one hundred and fifty short prayers instead, and the rosary grew out of that. It was sometimes called the poor man's psalter. There's a popular story that Mary gave the rosary to Saint Dominic. Historians tend to describe something slower: a prayer that grew over centuries, with many hands. And here's the plain secret of it. While the fingers and lips are busy with the words, the mind is free to go somewhere else: to think through scenes from the life of Jesus and Mary, called the mysteries. That's the real prayer. The beads just keep the hands busy.

segments.voice: Here's the practice. A forty-five-second sit, and your fingers do the counting. Rest one hand in your lap. With each breath out, touch your thumb to the next finger: index, middle, ring, little, and back again. Don't count out loud. Let your fingers keep track so your mind doesn't have to. If you pray, you can let each breath carry a short prayer. If not, just let each breath go. The bell holds the time.
The rosary, beads. A loop of five decades that keeps count, so the hands are busy and the heart is free. Tenth word.

11.title: the words, line by line, from Luke
11.hook: the words, line by line, from Luke

11.howItsDone: Catholics say the Hail Mary ten times on each decade of the rosary, and on its own at many moments of the day; its first half comes from Luke 1:28 and 1:42.

screen: `DAY ELEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the rosary beads: five decades, a counting string. Your line was: hands busy, heart free. Today, the words on those ten beads. Day eleven.
screen: `HANDS BUSY, HEART FREE.`

segments.voice: At a wake, a room full of voices runs it together until it sounds like one long word. A kid in Catholic school rattles it off before anyone can blink. In football, a quarterback throws the ball deep with no hope left, and that pass still gets called a Hail Mary. Said that fast, it's easy to miss where the words came from, and who said them first. Half the prayer isn't new at all. It's lifted, line by line, from the first chapter of Luke's Gospel. Today, slowly.
screen: `ONE LONG WORD AT A WAKE.` → `A HAIL MARY PASS.` → `LIFTED FROM LUKE.`

segments.voice: The first line belongs to an angel. Remember day six, Gabriel in the room in Nazareth. In the Douay-Rheims Bible, his first words are: "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee: blessed art thou among women." Hail is just an old hello. Full of grace is your first word, on day one: a gift given, filled to the brim. The next line belongs to a relative. A little later in Luke, Mary goes to visit her cousin Elizabeth, who's also pregnant, and Elizabeth cries out: "Blessed art thou among women, and blessed is the fruit of thy womb." Over the centuries Christians put those two greetings side by side, an angel's and a cousin's, and added two names: Mary, right after the angel's hail, and Jesus at the end. That's the whole first half. Every word of it, apart from those two names, is from Luke. Then the prayer turns. The second half isn't scripture. It's the Church speaking, and it came into the prayer later. It goes: Holy Mary, Mother of God, pray for us sinners, now and at the hour of our death. Amen. Listen to the shape. The first half says hello. The second half asks for something. And what it asks is small and huge at once: pray for us. Now, and at the very end. Catholics aren't asking Mary to do what only God does. They're asking her to pray with them, the way you'd ask anyone you trust to pray for you. On the rosary it's said ten times in each decade. A greeting, then a request, again and again, like a heartbeat, while the mind thinks about Jesus. Say it fast and it's a blur. Say it slowly and you're standing in two rooms in Luke's Gospel.
screen: `AN ANGEL'S HELLO.` · `A COUSIN'S BLESSING.` · `THEN THE CHURCH ASKS.` · `PRAY FOR US, NOW AND AT THE END.` · then, large: `A GREETING, THEN A REQUEST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. A forty-five-second sit. Let your breath slow down. On the breath in, think of a greeting: hello to someone you love. On the breath out, think of a request: one thing you need right now. In, a greeting. Out, a request. If you pray the Hail Mary, you can say it once, as slowly as you've ever said it. The bell holds the time.
The rosary, the Hail Mary. An angel's hello and a cousin's blessing from Luke, then the Church's request: pray for us. Eleventh word.

12.title: the most misunderstood room in the building
12.hook: the most misunderstood room in the building
12.carry: say it out loud, then it's smaller
12.tomorrow: the obligation nobody explains as a gift
12.howItsDone: Catholics go to confession with a priest, anonymously behind a screen or face to face, name their sins, receive a small penance, and hear the words of absolution; many go before Christmas and Easter, and some go monthly.

screen: `DAY TWELVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Hail Mary: an angel's hello, a cousin's blessing, then pray for us. Your line: a greeting then a request, ten times over on the beads. Did you greet someone first? Day twelve.
screen: `A GREETING, THEN A REQUEST.`

segments.voice: You know the scene from a hundred movies. A dark wooden booth. A little sliding window with a screen. A shadowy priest on one side, and someone on the other whispering, forgive me, Father, for I have sinned. In the movies it's usually a gangster, and the scene is tense, or it's a joke. Most people who've never been inside imagine something between a courtroom and a trap. Somebody listening, judging, taking notes. It might be the most misunderstood room in the building. Today, what actually happens in there, and why Catholics say people walk out lighter than they went in.
screen: `A DARK WOODEN BOOTH.` → `FORGIVE ME, FATHER.` → `A COURTROOM, OR A TRAP?`

segments.voice: Catholics call it the sacrament of reconciliation, or penance, and most just call it confession. Here's where it comes from. On Easter night in John's Gospel, the same scene as the peace from day four, the risen Jesus breathes on his friends and says, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "Whose sins you shall forgive, they are forgiven them." Catholics believe that from that moment, forgiveness was meant to be heard out loud, through a person, not only thought about privately. The letter of James says it too: "Confess therefore your sins one to another." So what happens in there? You go in. You can kneel behind the screen and stay anonymous, or sit face to face; it's your choice. You say how long it's been. Then you say what you've done wrong, plainly, in your own words. The priest listens. He might give some advice. He gives you a penance, usually a prayer or a small act to make things right. You say you're sorry, and he says the words of absolution, forgiving your sins in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. That sign again, from day two. It often takes about five minutes. And one rule is absolute. It's called the seal of confession. A priest may never reveal what he hears, to anyone, for any reason. Priests have gone to prison rather than break it. Catholics say part of the gift is simply this: you say it out loud to another human being, and it stops living only in your head. What was huge and shapeless in the dark at two in the morning has edges once it's spoken. It gets smaller. And then you hear someone say, out loud, that you're forgiven.
screen: `WHOSE SINS YOU SHALL FORGIVE.` · `BEHIND A SCREEN OR FACE TO FACE.` · `THE SEAL: NEVER REVEALED.` · `SPOKEN, IT HAS EDGES.` · then, large: `YOU'RE FORGIVEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. A forty-five-second sit. Think of one thing you're carrying that you've never said out loud. You don't have to say it now. Just name it to yourself, in one plain sentence, in your own words. Then breathe out slowly and notice whether it feels any different once it has a name. If you pray, you can hand it to God. The bell holds the time.
Confession. The sacrament of reconciliation: saying it out loud, and hearing out loud that you're forgiven. Twelfth word.

13.title: the obligation nobody explains as a gift
13.hook: the obligation nobody explains as a gift

13.howItsDone: Catholics are asked to attend Mass every Sunday (or on Saturday evening) and on certain holy days, and to keep the day for worship, family and rest as far as they can.

segments.voice: Yesterday, confession, the most misunderstood room in the building. Your line was: say it out loud, then it's smaller. Did anything get smaller? Day thirteen.
screen: `SAY IT OUT LOUD.`

segments.voice: Being woken up too early. Scratchy church clothes. A parent at the bottom of the stairs saying, we're going, it's an obligation. That's how some people who grew up Catholic remember Sunday. The Sunday obligation: Catholics are asked to go to Mass every Sunday, and to a kid it can sound like homework for the soul. Meanwhile the rest of the week is full. The phone that never stops. The laundry. The emails that arrive on Saturday night. What if the obligation was never meant as homework? Today, Sunday, explained as a gift.
screen: `SCRATCHY CHURCH CLOTHES.` → `HOMEWORK FOR THE SOUL?` → `SUNDAY, EXPLAINED AS A GIFT.`

segments.voice: Start at the very beginning of the Bible. In Genesis, God makes the world in six days, and then, in the Douay-Rheims Bible, "he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had done." God rests. Not, the tradition says, because he's tired. In the story, the day of rest is built into the world like a beam into a house. For the Jewish people it became the Sabbath, the seventh day, kept from sunset Friday to sunset Saturday, and Jewish families keep it still. Then something happened on a different day. All four Gospels put the empty tomb on the first day of the week, the day after the Sabbath. In the Acts of the Apostles, Christians gather on that first day to break bread. And the last book of the Bible uses a new name, which Christians came to give that day: "I was in the spirit on the Lord's day." In Latin, dies Domini, the Lord's day. In Spanish it's still domingo, in Italian domenica. An early Christian named Justin Martyr described it for outsiders: on the day called Sunday, everyone gathers, the memoirs of the apostles or the writings of the prophets are read, bread and wine are brought and blessed, and there's a collection for widows and orphans. That's recognizably the Mass from days three to five. So why call it an obligation? Catholics say it's the way the Church makes sure the gift actually gets opened. Left alone, a week fills every hour. The obligation holds one day open: for worship, for family, for rest, for a long meal. Sunday Mass can also be kept on Saturday evening, at what's called the vigil. The idea underneath is simple. One day a week isn't yours to fill.

segments.voice: Here's the practice. A forty-five-second sit, and for these forty-five seconds, you have nothing to do. Nothing to fill. Put the phone face down, or out of reach. Let your hands rest open. Every time your mind reaches for a task, notice it, and set it down for later. If you pray, you can offer the time to God. If not, just let it be empty. The bell holds the time.
Sunday. The Lord's day, the day of the empty tomb, the day the Church keeps open for worship and rest. Thirteenth word.

14.title: the family word he chose

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sunday, the gift inside the obligation. Your line was: one day that isn't yours to fill. And that's two weeks. This week: Francis, candles, the beads, the Hail Mary, confession, Sunday. Day fourteen.

segments.voice: A boss gets the best email voice. A judge gets your honor. A king, in the old days, got your majesty, said from the knees. The more powerful someone is, the more careful and formal the words. In Luke's Gospel, a disciple asks Jesus: teach us to pray. How do you talk to the one who made the stars? Titles, you might expect. A long list of them. Instead he gives them a prayer that begins with a family word. It's the prayer on the single beads of the rosary, from day ten. Today, the family word he chose.
screen: `YOUR HONOR. YOUR MAJESTY.` → `TEACH US TO PRAY.` → `A FAMILY WORD.`

segments.voice: In Matthew's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims Bible, it starts: "Our Father who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name." Father. Behind the Greek of the Gospels, some scholars hear the Aramaic word abba. Mark's Gospel keeps that word untranslated, on the night before he died, when Jesus prays in the garden: "Abba, Father, all things are possible to thee." Abba is the word a son or daughter uses. Not a title. A relationship. And then look at the word before it: our. Not my Father. Our. Read it closely and there isn't a single I or me in the whole prayer. Give us. Forgive us. Lead us. Deliver us. Someone praying it alone at night still prays in the plural, standing in a crowd they can't see. That's the family word doing its work twice: God is not a stranger, and neither is the person next to you. Remember the handshake from day four? In the Mass, the whole room prays the Our Father together right before it. Catholics call it the Lord's Prayer too, and for a long time they prayed it in Latin: Pater noster, our Father. One difference shows up in other churches. Churches that learned the prayer from the King James Bible end with, for thine is the kingdom, the power and the glory. The King James prints that line in Matthew; the Douay-Rheims, translated from the Latin, ends at deliver us from evil, and so do Catholics. At Mass, the priest adds a short prayer, and then everyone says a version of it together. Same prayer, two old habits. And it opens with a family word.
screen: `ABBA — FATHER, AT HOME.` · `OUR, NOT MY.` · `NO I, NO ME.` · `PATER NOSTER.` · then, large: `NOT A STRANGER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice for the end of week two. A forty-five-second sit. Say just the first two words, slowly, out loud or silently: our Father. On our, think of someone you'd rather not include in that word, and include them anyway. On Father, notice how different it sounds from a title. If you pray the whole prayer, you can pray it once, very slowly. The bell holds the time.
The Our Father. The prayer Jesus taught, opening with a family word, and with no I or me in it anywhere. Fourteenth word.
screen: `THE OUR FATHER — your 14th word`.

segments.voice: Your line: not a stranger. Today, treat one stranger like family for a moment: a name, a thank-you, a question about their day. Day fourteen. Two weeks.
